G04-T13.close: Whitespace is the clearest case in this group of "invisible in the query tool, catastrophic in production" — the value looks fine on screen and breaks every comparison anyway. Special / Control Character in Text Field is next, going even further into characters you genuinely cannot see at all.

G04-T14.open: If whitespace was invisible, this lesson is about characters that are truly invisible — not just visually similar to something else, but literally zero-width or non-printing.

questions.q: Why does detecting control characters (CHAR 1 through CHAR 8, for example) require PATINDEX combined with CHAR(), instead of a literal character range typed directly into a LIKE pattern?
choices: LIKE's bracket range syntax needs the CHAR() function to build a range using actual control-character codes, since you can't type an unprintable character literally into a pattern string
PATINDEX is simply a faster version of LIKE with no functional difference
Control characters cannot be detected by any SQL Server function
LIKE only supports checking for letters and digits, never any other character type
questions.right: Exactly — you can't type CHAR(1) as a literal character in your SQL source code the way you can type 'A'. Building the range dynamically with CHAR() is how you reference an unprintable character at all.
questions.wrong: You can't literally type an unprintable control character into your SQL source code the way you'd type a letter or digit. `PATINDEX('%[' + CHAR(1) + '-' + CHAR(8) + ']%', col)` builds the bracket range as a string at runtime using the CHAR() function to reference those specific unprintable codes — that's the only way to express "match any character in this control-character range" when the range itself contains characters you can't type directly.

questions.q: Why is a BOM (Byte Order Mark) character at the start of a field dangerous, given that it's completely invisible?
choices: It becomes an invisible extra character at the very start of the string, causing exact string comparisons to silently fail — 'Widget A' no longer equals a BOM-prefixed 'Widget A' even though they look identical
The BOM character actively deletes the rest of the string it's attached to
SQL Server automatically rejects any field starting with a BOM
BOM characters only ever appear at the end of a string, never the start
questions.right: Exactly — this is the same invisible-but-breaks-comparison problem as whitespace and non-breaking spaces, in its purest form. Nothing about the BOM is visible in a query tool, but it's a real extra character that string equality checks will catch.
questions.wrong: A BOM is a zero-width character (U+FEFF) that some files place at the start to declare their encoding. When it lands as the first character of a database field, it's invisible to the eye in most tools but is a genuinely different character from a nonexistent one — so an exact-match comparison between 'Widget A' and BOM+'Widget A' fails, even though they render identically on screen. It's the same class of problem as whitespace padding, just harder to spot.

questions.q: What does a doubled HTML entity like `&amp;` reveal about how the data got into that state?
choices: An HTML-encoding function was applied to text that was already HTML-encoded, encoding the ampersand a second time
The original text simply contained the literal characters '&amp;' typed by a user
It indicates the field was decoded twice, not encoded
It's a random data corruption with no identifiable cause
questions.right: Right — `&amp;` is what you get when `&` gets encoded to `&` once, and then something encodes that ALREADY-encoded text a second time, turning the `&` inside `&` into `&` too.
questions.wrong: This is a specific, diagnosable pattern: a plain `&` gets HTML-encoded once into `&` — correct so far. But if an encoding function runs a SECOND time on text that's already encoded, it encodes the `&` inside `&` again, producing `&amp;`. The lesson notes the visible symptom is the entity text literally appearing on the rendered page (users see "&" instead of "&") — a clear signal of a two-pass encoding bug in the pipeline.

G04-T14.close: Between whitespace, non-breaking spaces, and BOM characters, you've now got a genuine toolkit for the class of bug that's completely invisible in a query result grid. Boolean / Flag Field Format is next — a much more visible problem, but one that silently breaks WHERE clauses in a different way.

G04-T15.open: Different kind of danger here: nothing is invisible, nothing fails to parse. The problem is that four different teams each picked their own perfectly reasonable way to write "yes" and "no."

questions.q: Why does `WHERE IsActive = 1` silently miss records stored as 'Y', 'true', or 'yes', instead of raising an error?
choices: The comparison only matches rows where the value is literally the integer 1 — 'Y', 'true', and 'yes' are different values entirely, so they're excluded from the result set with no error, no warning, nothing
SQL Server automatically converts 'Y' and 'true' to 1 before comparing, so nothing should actually be missed
The query would fail to run at all if the column contains mixed representations
IsActive = 1 only works correctly on tables with fewer than 100 rows
questions.right: Exactly — and this silence is exactly why the lesson calls it one of the most dangerous classes of error. The query runs successfully, returns a plausible-looking result set, and simply never includes the rows stored under a different true/false convention.
questions.wrong: `WHERE IsActive = 1` only matches rows where the stored value is literally the integer 1. A row storing 'Y', 'true', or 'yes' simply doesn't equal 1 — it's excluded from the results, with the query running successfully and returning no error at all. That silence is what makes this dangerous: the query looks like it worked, the results look plausible, and there's nothing to alert you that a chunk of valid data was quietly left out.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist on profiling all distinct values (Step 2) before writing any UPDATE to normalize the column?
choices: Profiling first reveals the full picture of every variant actually present, preventing an obscure value like 'T' or 'enabled' from being missed by an UPDATE that only anticipated the common cases
SQL Server requires a SELECT to run before any UPDATE statement for syntax reasons
Profiling automatically fixes the data without needing an UPDATE at all
It has no real benefit over writing the UPDATE directly
questions.right: Right — a normalization UPDATE is only as good as its coverage. Profiling first is what tells you whether your UPDATE's IN-list actually covers every variant that exists, instead of just the ones you happened to think of.
questions.wrong: The risk the lesson names directly: writing a normalization UPDATE without profiling first means you might handle 'Y', 'yes', and 'true' but completely miss an obscure variant like 'T' or 'enabled' that also exists in the data. Profiling every distinct value first — Step 2 — shows you the full contamination picture, so the eventual fix actually covers everything that's really there instead of just the cases you assumed.

questions.q: What long-term fix does the lesson recommend after the column has been normalized to 0/1?
choices: Change the column's data type to BIT, which only accepts 0 and 1 and prevents future format drift back into mixed representations
Delete the column entirely and never store this information again
Add a comment to the column explaining what values are allowed
Rename the column so future developers know to be careful with it
questions.right: Exactly — normalizing the existing data fixes today's problem; changing the column type is what stops the same drift from happening again the next time a new team or integration touches this column.
questions.wrong: Normalizing the existing rows to 0/1 fixes the data that already exists, but doesn't stop a fourth team or a future integration from introducing yet another convention next year. The lesson's long-term recommendation is changing the column's type to BIT (`ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN IsActive BIT NOT NULL`), which structurally only accepts 0 and 1 — making the drift this lesson describes impossible to reintroduce at the schema level.

G04-T15.close: One more lesson to close out this half — a full-circle look at enumerated values, one more time, with a sharper business-rule angle.

G04-T16.open: Last lesson before the halfway break. Same theme as the boolean lesson — a value outside the approved set — but this time the approved set has more than two options, which changes how you validate it.

questions.q: Why does the query use a table variable (`@ApprovedDepts`) holding the approved department list, instead of hard-coding the list directly inside every WHERE clause?
choices: It separates the approved values from the validation logic — adding or removing an approved value means changing it in one place, not hunting down every WHERE clause that repeats the list
Table variables run faster than any other SQL Server construct
A hard-coded IN list is not valid SQL syntax
Table variables are required whenever more than 3 values need checking
questions.right: Exactly — this is a maintainability decision, not a performance one. One list, referenced everywhere it's needed, means one place to update when the business adds a new department.
questions.wrong: If the approved list were hard-coded into every WHERE clause across five different queries, adding a new department would mean finding and editing all five. Storing it once in `@ApprovedDepts` and referencing that in every check means there's exactly one place to update — the validation logic itself doesn't need to change when the business adds or removes an approved value.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist on profiling all distinct Department values (Step 2) before fixing any of them?
choices: Profiling first reveals the full picture — without it, you might fix the obvious 'IT' but completely miss a less obvious invalid variant like 'Information Technology'
SQL Server requires a profiling step before any UPDATE can run
Profiling automatically corrects every invalid value without needing a fix
There is no real benefit — it's an optional convenience step
questions.right: Right — same principle as the boolean-flag lesson, applied here: without seeing every distinct value first, you're guessing at what needs fixing instead of knowing.
questions.wrong: This is the same lesson as the boolean-flag check, applied to a bigger set of options: without profiling every distinct value that actually exists, you're fixing based on assumption. You might catch the obvious 'IT' but never notice 'Information Technology' sitting in the same column as a completely separate invalid variant, because you never looked at the full list of what's really there.

questions.q: What long-term, database-level fix does the lesson recommend for an enumerated column like Department?
choices: A CHECK constraint that restricts the column to only the approved values, preventing any future invalid value from ever being inserted
Deleting the Department column entirely from the table
Converting the column to store department names as pure numbers
Renaming the column so it's harder for other teams to write to it
questions.right: Exactly — same pattern as the BIT-type recommendation for booleans: fix the existing data, then change the schema itself so the same class of drift can't happen again.
questions.wrong: Just like the boolean lesson recommended converting to BIT to prevent future drift, this lesson recommends a `CHECK` constraint — `CHECK (Department IN ('Sales','Marketing',...))` — which stops any future INSERT or UPDATE from ever storing a value outside the approved list. Cleaning up today's bad data fixes the past; the CHECK constraint is what prevents the same problem from quietly recurring.

G04-T16.close: That's the halfway point of Format/Pattern — 16 lessons down, 16 to go. You've now covered universal formats (email, phone, dates), country-specific structures (postcodes, IBANs, NINOs), organization-defined codes (SKUs), and the invisible/silent failure modes (whitespace, control characters, boolean and enum drift). Second half picks up next session.
